title: The Dire Dawa Hotel Room Where Dahabshiil's Transfers Began
dek: In August 1988, having lost his warehouses in the fighting at Burao, Mohamed Said Duale began carrying refugees' money from Dubai to the Ethiopian border.

story.event: Starting to collect and deliver refugees' remittances from a hotel room in Dire Dawa after losing his Burao business
story.summary: In August 1988, after fighting in Burao destroyed his wholesale trading business, Mohamed Said Duale reached Dire Dawa in Ethiopia with about $100. Somalis in the Emirates asked him to collect money for relatives who had fled; he routed it through Djibouti, froze his customer list at a few hundred names and delivered the cash himself near the border. He traced the remittance company Dahabshiil to those weeks.
paragraphs: In early August 1988, Mohamed Said Duale reached Dire Dawa, in eastern Ethiopia, on a travel permit shared with about a dozen other Somalis. By his own account he had about a hundred dollars. Until that year he had been one of the leading wholesale traders in Burao, in northern Somalia. Then, from late May, fighting between the rebel Somali National Movement and government forces tore through the town. He led his family and neighbours out on foot through the bush, and his warehouses were looted. What remained, he later told the scholar Ahmed Samatar, was 30,000 dirhams that people in Dubai owed him.

In Dire Dawa, northerners crowded a small house used by the movement's representatives, waiting for calls from relatives abroad on its single telephone. After two frustrating days, Duale took an inexpensive hotel room with its own phone and rang a contact in Dubai. The money owed to him began to arrive. Then Somalis in the Emirates asked for something new: would he collect what they were sending to relatives who had fled, and deliver it, for a small commission? He had never dealt in money exchange, he said, but he agreed.

The work soon outgrew him. He borrowed the fax machine at a prominent Somali trader's office until his messages clogged its line, then used the hotel's. When his list passed a few hundred names, he froze it. Harari merchants in the city told him Djibouti was the place for such transfers, so he moved a small sum from Dubai to an Indian money changer there, who passed it to a clothes shop in Dire Dawa whose back room paid out in Ethiopian birr. Duale then travelled to a village near the border, sent word to everyone on his list and handed each their money, selling rice to some of them.

He later said the recipients thanked him for being prompt and honest, and that word of it travelled back to Dubai, where more money was entrusted to him. He traced Dahabshiil, which by the 2010s worked in more than a hundred countries, to those weeks in Dire Dawa, calling it "an opportunity born out of a catastrophe."

quote.text: show yourself to me to be faithful, modest, and steady; show me that you have friendly opinions; show that your cask has no hole in it; and you will see how I shall not wait for you to trust me with your own affairs
quote.locator: Book IV, Chapter 13, "Against or to those who readily tell their own affairs"
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: Epictetus was talking about confidences, but his watertight cask fits money as well. Duale could not advertise his way to trust in 1988. He could only deliver what he was given, stop taking what he could not carry, and let the people in Dubai come back with more.

reflection: One detail in this story is easy to pass over: when the list reached a few hundred names, Duale stopped adding to it. He had just lost almost everything and needed the commissions, yet he chose to serve fewer people well rather than let more of them down.

You will have weeks when every request looks like a chance you cannot afford to miss. Saying yes to all of them can feel generous, but a promise made while stretched too thin leaks like wine from a cracked cask. People remember what arrived more than what was offered. Before taking on more, it is fair to ask whether you can still carry what you already hold.
invitation: Look at what you have promised other people this week. If there is one thing you cannot deliver well, tell that person today, plainly, and give them a date you can keep.

sources.title: The Making of Dahabshiil: A Brief Interview (Bildhaan: An International Journal of Somali Studies, vol. 21, 2021)
sources.supports: Duale's own account (interview of 2019, conducted in Somali and translated by Samatar; full text in the PDF linked from this page): his Burao wholesale business; the SNM fighting in Burao and his walk out of the town with family and neighbours, avoiding the road; warehouses looted; the 30,000 dirhams owed to him in Dubai; the shared travel permit from Jigjiga and arrival in Dire Dawa in early August 1988; about one hundred dollars; the queue at the single telephone in the house used by SNM representatives; the hotel room with a telephone and the call to Dubai; the request from Somalis in the Emirates that he collect money for relatives, for a small commission; never having dealt in money exchange; the borrowed fax at Hogsaday's office and then the hotel's; freezing the list after a few hundred names; the Harari merchants' advice about Djibouti, the Indian money changer and the Dire Dawa clothes shop paying out in birr; delivering the money and selling rice in a village near the border; recipients' thanks and more money entrusted to him in Dubai; tracing Dahabshiil to that moment; 'an opportunity born out of a catastrophe'.

sources.title: A Thread of Hope
sources.supports: Duale's Burao trading business before the war; the 1988 government assault on northern towns and flight into Ethiopia; that he launched Dahabshiil in Dire Dawa using his trade networks; that he served refugees from all clans; Dahabshiil's later reach (outlets in 128 countries in 2014).

cross_checks.claim: Fighting reached Burao in May 1988 and Duale's trading business there was lost
The remittance business began in Dire Dawa, Ethiopia, after Duale fled Burao
In the early days Duale delivered the money to recipients himself
Dahabshiil's roots are a trading business started around 1970, which became a remittance business only after the war

research_notes: The slate placed this episode in 1991 and called it hard-responsibility; Duale's own account dates the start of the remittance work to August 1988 in Dire Dawa, Ethiopia, after he lost his Burao business, so the date, country and arc (change-of-direction) were corrected. Most of the story rests on one founder interview, conducted in Somali in 2019 and translated by Ahmed I. Samatar (Bildhaan vol. 21, 2021; the landing page links the full-text PDF at https://macalester.edu/international-studies/wp-content/uploads/sites/569/2017/10/Samatar_The-Making-of-Dahabshiil-A-Brief-Interview.pdf), and the prose attributes it to him. Dates: the interview gives the SNM entry into Burao as 'May 27, 1987' but later says the violence in Burao 'started in May 1988' and that he reached Dire Dawa in early August 1988; Human Rights Watch (1989) and every other source put the northern offensive in May 1988, so the story says late May 1988. Warehouses: he speaks of three full bakhaars in one place and five in another, so the story gives no number. Refugee numbers differ: HRW (1989) says some 450,000 fled to Ethiopia, Djibouti and Kenya; GOOD (2014) says some 800,000 fled into Ethiopia; Somaliland Current (2024) says about half a million left; the story gives none. GOOD says Duale settled in Dire Dawa with his family and used bike messengers; in his own account he left the family in a rural outpost, travelled alone and delivered the first payments himself, so the story follows his account. Founding: the company and Abdirashid Duale date Dahabshiil to a shop in Burao in 1970 (Duale says his first trading venture was in early 1970); the remittance business is dated by Duale to 1988, and the story makes that distinction. Scale: GOOD gives 128 countries (2014), Somaliland Current 126 (2024) and the company's site 'over 100'; the story says more than a hundred. Staff figures differ widely (about 1,000 in money transfer per Duale in 2019, about 2,000 per How we made it in Africa in 2010, about 10,000 per Somaliland Current in 2024) and are not used. The 'Hogsaday' office is described only as a prominent Somali trader's office. Later regulatory scrutiny of Dahabshiil and of Somali remittances is outside this episode and is not discussed. The Epictetus passage is about whom to trust with confidences; it is applied to money by analogy, and the chapter number follows the standard numbering of the Discourses (the Gutenberg selection prints chapter titles only).
